segments.t: Continuing their talk in the kitchen, Dmitry Nagiyev reveals why tomorrow's guest matters so much: a famous producer is casting a new adaptation of War and Peace, and Nagiyev wants the role of Napoleon. Listen to their exchange in Russian.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
Now let's go back through their exchange line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'I can see by your eyes that you don't understand.' Dmitry keeps the sentence short and direct, relying on Russian case endings to show how the words connect.
'A film producer is coming.' Dmitry keeps the sentence short and direct, relying on Russian case endings to show how the words connect.
'He wants to film War and Peace.' Dmitry uses natural conversational word order here to highlight the most important part of the reply.
'With me in the leading role.' In spoken Russian, Dmitry omits unnecessary linking verbs so the key idea lands immediately.
'I am going to play Napoleon.' Dmitry keeps the sentence short and direct, relying on Russian case endings to show how the words connect.
'You have to feed him so well.' Notice how Dmitry pairs a modal word or finite verb with an infinitive to express the action.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
'I am begging you, Vitya, don't mess this up.' Dmitry uses natural conversational word order here to highlight the most important part of the reply.
'Yes, got it.' Chef Viktor keeps the sentence short and direct, relying on Russian case endings to show how the words connect.
'What did I just say?' Dmitry raises the pitch on the key word to turn this short Russian clause into a direct question.
'Onto the French throne.' In spoken Russian, Chef Viktor omits unnecessary linking verbs so the key idea lands immediately.
'I said do not mess it up.' Dmitry keeps the sentence short and direct, relying on Russian case endings to show how the words connect.
'Ah, that too.' In spoken Russian, Chef Viktor omits unnecessary linking verbs so the key idea lands immediately. Now let's hear the entire conversation once more from start to finish.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.

That finishes Nagiyev's grand Napoleon speech and his warning to Chef Barinov not to mess up the dinner. Pay attention to how Russian expresses future plans and urgent requests. See you in the next scene.
